''' Kristi S. Anseth''' (born 1969) is the Tisone Distinguished Professor of [[Chemical engineering|Chemical]] and [[Biological Engineering]], an Associate Professor of [[Surgery]], and a Howard Hughes Medical Investigator at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]].<ref name="Swanson"/><ref name="Purdue">{{cite web|url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/Engr/People/Awards/Institutional/DEA/DEA_2012/Anseth |title=Kristi S. Anseth|website=Purdue University College of Engineering}}</ref>  Her main research interests are the design of synthetic [[biomaterials]] using [[hydrogels]], [[tissue engineering]], and [[regenerative medicine]].

Anseth was elected as a member into the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2009 for pioneering the rational design of biomaterials for tissue engineering, drug delivery, and biosensing applications.

==Early life and education==
Kristi Anseth grew up in [[Williston, North Dakota]]. She played on both the volleyball and basketball teams at the [[Williston State College|University of North Dakota-Williston]], earning the honor of Academic All-American in her second year.<ref name="Simpson">{{cite news|last1=Simpson|first1=Kevin|title=Brilliant mind, noble cause|url=http://www.denverpost.com/2008/03/24/brilliant-mind-noble-cause/|access-date=25 October 2016|work=The Denver Post|date=March 24, 2008}}</ref>

Kristi Anseth transferred to [[Purdue University]] where she began her research career as an undergraduate student in the lab of [[Nicholas A. Peppas]], receiving her Bachelor of Science in Chemical Engineering in 1992.<ref name="Purdue"/>  She obtained her PhD in 1994, working under [[Christopher N. Bowman]], himself a former graduate student of Nicholas Peppas, at the University of Colorado.<ref name="Simpson"/>

==Career==
After post-doctoral work with [[Robert Langer]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]  and [[Thomas Cech]], Anseth became an assistant professor at the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder in 1996.<ref name="Davidson"/> She currently leads the Anseth Research Group as the Tisone Distinguished Professor of [[Chemical engineering|Chemical]] and [[Biological Engineering]].<ref name=Anseth>{{cite web|title=Kristi S. Anseth|url=http://www.colorado.edu/chbe/kristi-s-anseth|website=Chemical and Biological Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder|date=2016-12-07}}</ref> She serves on Purdue's College of Engineering Advisory Council.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/Engr/People/Committees/EAC|title=Engineering Advisory Council - Active|work=College of Engineering - Purdue University|access-date=2017-10-01|language=en}}</ref>

Anseth is working at the intersection of [[materials science]], [[chemistry]] and [[biology]],<ref name="Flanagan">{{cite news|last1=Flanagan|first1=Dave|title=Kristi S. Anseth to Receive MRS Mid-Career Researcher Award|url=http://materialsviews.com/kristi-s-anseth-to-receive-mrs-mid-career-researcher-award/|access-date=26 October 2016|work=Materials Views|date=April 4, 2012}}</ref> studying natural and synthetic [[hydrogels]] and using [[biomaterials]] to create an [[extracellular matrix]] to support [[3D cell culture|three-dimensional cell enculturation]].<ref name="HHMI">{{cite web|title=Kristi S. Anseth, PhD|url=http://www.hhmi.org/scientists/kristi-s-anseth|website=Howard Hughes Medical Institute|access-date=26 October 2016}}</ref><ref name="Tibbitt">{{cite journal|last1=Tibbitt|first1=Mark W.|last2=Anseth|first2=Kristi S.|title=Hydrogels as extracellular matrix mimics for 3D cell culture|journal=Biotechnology and Bioengineering|date=1 July 2009|volume=103|issue=4|pages=655–663|doi=10.1002/bit.22361|pmc=2997742|pmid=19472329}}</ref>

Anseth is developing photopolymers that will change from soft to hard in response to cues such as [[ultraviolet light]], and then degrade predictably over time.<ref name="Innovators"/> Such materials could be used to for orthopedic repairs, functioning as a replacement for damaged areas of bone and then slowly being replaced by regrowth of natural material as the body heals. Her pioneering approach applies [[photopolymerization]] and [[photodegradation]] to enable precise control in space and time of hydrogels' structure and composition. This research involves fundamental investigations into the molecular dynamics of processes at the cell-biomaterial interface.<ref name="Flanagan"/>

Anseth is also working on the [[tissue engineering]] of biomaterials for the replacement of cartilage and heart valves.<ref name="HHMI"/> By combining photopolymers and lab-grown cartilage her lab is creating living replacements for worn-out joints. The problem is more difficult than replacing bone because the cartilage in joints, unlike bone, does not have the ability to regrow.<ref name="Innovators"/><ref name="Kim">{{cite journal|last1=Kim|first1=Iris L.|last2=Mauck|first2=Robert L.|last3=Burdick|first3=Jason A.|title=Hydrogel design for cartilage tissue engineering: A case study with hyaluronic acid|journal=Biomaterials|date=December 2011|volume=32|issue=34|pages=8771–8782|doi=10.1016/j.biomaterials.2011.08.073|pmc=3183132|pmid=21903262}}</ref>

She has published more than 250 papers and filed for at least 18 patents.<ref name="VP"/>  She has been involved in editorial activities of journals including ''[[Biomacromolecules]]'', ''Journal of Biomedical Materials Research — Part A'', ''[[Acta Biomaterialia]]'', ''[[Progress in Materials Science]]'', ''[[Biotechnology and Bioengineering]]''<ref name="Bailey">{{cite news|title=Dr. Kristi Anseth Wins 2013 James E. Bailey Award Winner|url=http://www.aiche.org/sbe/about/press/releases/08-20-2013/dr-kristi-anseth-wins-2013-james-e-bailey-award-winner|access-date=26 October 2016|work=Society for Biological Engineering|date=August 20, 2013}}</ref> and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Ri|last2=Yang|first2=Zhongguang|last3=Luo|first3=Jiren|last4=Hsing|first4=I.-Ming|last5=Sun|first5=Fei|date=2017-06-06|title=B12-dependent photoresponsive protein hydrogels for controlled stem cell/protein release|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=114|issue=23|pages=5912–5917|doi=10.1073/pnas.1621350114|issn=0027-8424|pmid=28533376|pmc=5468657|doi-access=free}}</ref>  In September 2014, she was elected the Vice President/President-Elect of the [[Materials Research Society]] (MRS), serving as Vice President in 2015 and President in 2016.<ref name="VP">{{cite news|title=Materials Research Society President-Elect, Kristi S. Anseth, Named 2015 Bayer Distinguished Lecturer at Pitt|url=http://www.mrs.org/press-room/press-release-details-page/2015/04/20/materials-research-society-president-elect-kristi-s.-anseth-named-2015-bayer-distinguished-lecturer-at-pitt|access-date=26 October 2016|work=Materials Research Society|date=April 20, 2015}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==

In 1999, Anseth was named to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] [[Technology Review]] [[TR35|TR100]] as one of the top 100 innovators in the world under the age of 35.<ref name="Innovators">{{cite web |url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?trid=496 |title=1999 Young Innovators Under 35: Kristi Anseth, 31 |publisher=[[Technology Review]] |year=1999 |access-date=August 15, 2011 |archive-date=April 16, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110416123256/https://www.technologyreview.com/TR35/Profile.aspx?TRID=496 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Kristi Anseth was the first engineer, male or female, to be selected as a Howard Hughes Medical Investigator.<ref name="Davidson"/> At age 40, she was the youngest member ever to be elected to both the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2009)<ref name="NAE">{{cite web|url=http://www.nae.edu/MembersSection/Directory20412/30918.aspx |title=Dr. Kristi S. Anseth
|website=NAE Members}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Medicine|Institute of Medicine]] (2009<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=10122009a|title=Institute Of Medicine Elects 65 New Members, Five Foreign Associates|date=October 12, 2009|website=www8.nationalacademies.org|language=en|access-date=2020-03-03}}</ref>).<ref name="Purdue"/> In 2013, she was also elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.colorado.edu/chbe/2013/05/02/kristi-anseth-elected-national-academy-sciences|title=Kristi Anseth Elected to National Academy of Sciences|date=2013-05-02|work=Chemical and Biological Engineering|access-date=2017-10-01|language=en}}</ref>  She shares the distinction of being a member of all three with chemical engineers [[Cato Laurencin]], Robert S. Langer, Nicholas A. Peppas, [[Frances Arnold]], and [[Rakesh K. Jain]].  As of 2015, she was also named to the [[National Academy of Inventors]].<ref name="Inventors">{{cite web|title=Kristi Anseth named National Academy of Inventors Fellow|url=http://www.colorado.edu/chbe/2016/04/29/kristi-anseth-named-national-academy-inventors-fellow|website=Chemical and Biological Engineering University of Colorado Boulder|access-date=April 29, 2016|date=2016-04-29}}</ref>
She was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/news/2019-members-announcement|title=New 2019 Academy Members Announced|publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|date=April 17, 2019}}</ref>

Other awards and honors include: 
* 2024, [[VinFuture Prize]], Special Prize for Women Innovators, For Advancement in Design of Polymeric Biomaterials and Methods for Biomedical Applications
* 2020, [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science]]<ref>{{cite web | title=L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science International Awards 2022 | website=L&#039;Oréal Finance | date=1963-10-08 | url=https://www.loreal-finance.com/eng/news-event/loreal-unesco-women-science-international-awards-2022 | access-date=2025-03-25}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=22nd L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Awards recognizes five exceptional women researchers in the life sciences | website=unesco.org | url=https://en.unesco.org/news/22nd-loreal-unesco-women-science-awards-recognizes-five-exceptional-women-researchers-life | language=en| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200212142756/https://en.unesco.org/news/22nd-loreal-unesco-women-science-awards-recognizes-five-exceptional-women-researchers-life | archive-date=12 February 2020 | access-date=2025-03-25}}</ref>
* 2016, Honorary Doctorate, Purdue University, College of Engineering<ref name="32f64f">{{cite web|url = http://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/releases/2016/Q2/eli-lilly-leader,-distinguished-chemical-and-biological-engineering-stalwart-to-receive-purdue-honorary-doctorates.html | title = Eli Lilly leader, distinguished chemical and biological engineering stalwart to receive Purdue honorary doctorates | publisher = Purdue University | access-date = 2016-05-03 |author=Jim Bush}}</ref> 
* 2015, Bayer Distinguished Lectureship, [[University of Pittsburgh]]<ref name="Swanson">{{cite web|title=Renowned tissue engineering researcher Kristi Anseth from University of Colorado named 2015 Bayer Distinguished Lecturer at Pitt|url=http://www.engineering.pitt.edu/News/Renowned-tissue-engineering-researcher-Kristi-Anseth-from-University-of-Colorado-named-2015-Bayer-Distinguished-Lecturer-at-Pitt/|website=Swanson Engineering, PITT|date=January 22, 2015|access-date=25 October 2016|archive-date=26 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026081200/http://www.engineering.pitt.edu/News/Renowned-tissue-engineering-researcher-Kristi-Anseth-from-University-of-Colorado-named-2015-Bayer-Distinguished-Lecturer-at-Pitt/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2015, [[May Bonfils Stanton#Legacy|Bonfils-Stanton]] Awards, Science and Medicine honoree<ref name="Davidson">{{cite news|last1=Davidson|first1=Joanne|title=Dianne Reeves, Adele Phelan and Kristi Anseth receive 2015 Bonfils-Stanton Awards|url=http://blogs.denverpost.com/style/tag/dr-kristi-anseth/|access-date=25 October 2016|work=The Denver Post|date=May 13, 2015}}</ref>
* 2013, James E. Bailey Award, [[Society for Biological Engineering]]<ref name="Bailey"/>
* 2012, [[Colorado Women's Hall of Fame]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cogreatwomen.org/project/kristi-anseth/|title=Kristi S. Anseth is a pioneer in biomedical engineering, a leading researcher|website=Colorado Women's Hall of Fame|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-03}}</ref>
* 2012, Distinguished Engineering Alumni award, Purdue University<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/Engr/People/Awards/Institutional/DEA/DEA_2012/Anseth|title=Kristi S. Anseth|work=College of Engineering - Purdue University|access-date=2017-10-01|language=en}}</ref>
* 2009, Fellow of the [[Materials Research Society]]<ref name="MRS2009">{{cite web|title=2009 MRS Fellows|url=http://www.mrs.org/mrs-fellows-2009/|website=Materials Research Society|access-date=26 October 2016|archive-date=26 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026170919/http://www2.mrs.org/mrs-fellows-2009/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2008, Clemson Award for Basic Research from the Society for Biomaterials<ref name="Biomaterials">{{cite web|title=Awards and Recognition of Advancements in the Field of Biomaterials|url=https://www.biomaterials.org/awards/past-awardees|website=Society For Biomaterials|access-date=26 October 2016}}</ref>
* 2005, Elizabeth Gee Award, University of Colorado<ref name="Gee">{{cite web|title=Elizabeth D. Gee Memorial Lectureship Award|url=https://www.cu.edu/faculty-council/about-elizabeth-d-gee-memorial-lectureship-award|website=University of Colorado|access-date=26 October 2016|date=2014-01-27}}</ref>
* 2004, Alan T. Waterman Award, National Science Foundation<ref name="Waterman">{{cite web|title=Alan T. Waterman Award Recipients, 1976 - present|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/waterman/waterman_recipients.jsp|website=National Science Foundation|access-date=26 October 2016}}</ref>
* 2001, Outstanding Young Investigator Award, [[Materials Research Society]].<ref name=Outstanding>{{cite journal|website=Materials Research Society|title=Outstanding Young Investigator Award|url=http://www.mrs.org/oyi}}</ref>
